catalog_quote: [printed p. 12, sec. 2.1] There are sixteen letters in the alphabet of Fasu (Namo Me) which divide into five vowels and eleven consonants. There are also two pertinent tones at the word level and nasalization of vowels is contrastive with non-nasalized vowels. For more details see May-Loeweke, 1965. [p. 13] In the following list V stands for vowel. High and low tone is marked above the vowel and nasalization is marked below the vowel. V́ high tone on vowels of single syllable words is pronounced as a downglide. V́ high tone on vowels of syllables prior to the last syllable is pronounced as level high going to straight low tone on last syllable. V́ high tone on vowels of last syllable of words is pronounced as adownglide. V̄ low tone on vowels of single syllable words is pronounced as an upglide. V̄ low tone on vowels of syllables prior to last syllable is pronounced as level low tone going to a downglide on last syllable. V̄ low tone on vowels of last syllable of word is pronounced as an upglide. [p. 15, sec. 2.2] In the following list tone is contrasted. This contrast is not underlined. nómo 'you' nōmo 'I' kasé 'underarm' kasē 'pith' [both vowels of the kase pair nasalised] seré 'mountain ridge' serē 'shoots' sére 'sun' tēraka 'fold' né 'you' nē 'mosquito'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Fasu is a word-tone language: each word carries one tonal specification, High or Low, realised on a single marked syllable; the position of that syllable is lexical and may be any syllable of the word (p. 15 minimal set: seré 'mountain ridge', serē 'shoots', sére 'sun'), and the pitch of the remaining syllables follows from it (pre-marked high stays level high then falls to low on the final; marked final/monosyllabic H = downglide, L = upglide). May & Loeweke 1965 (seen only second-hand via Cahill 2011 and Hyman 2006/2009) call this marked syllable the 'nuclear' (stressed) syllable: stress placement is unpredictable (any syllable of 1-3-syllable words) and the H/L contrast lives only on the stressed syllable, other syllables being toneless/predictable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in the 1980 grammar; second-hand reports mention none.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the grammar notes dialect differences (Kaipu/Sisipia/Kewotiki vs southern) only for vowel-harmony suffixes and vocabulary, not prosody.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms ('tones at the word level'); realisation rules refer to position of the marked syllable relative to the word's last syllable. The explicit equation marked syllable = stressed syllable comes from the 1965 Anthropological Linguistics article, not opened here.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1980 grammar covers Fasu = Namo Me as a whole (Lake Kutubu / Kikori, Southern Highlands & Gulf), data 1961-1976, noting a northern (Kaipu-Sisipia-Kewotiki) vs southern dialect split that is not said to affect prosody; glottocode fasu1242 applies directly. Hyman cites the 1965 paper as '1964'; same work (Anthropological Linguistics 7(5)).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Fasu is described as having two contrastive tones (high vs low) operating at the word level, marked on one vowel of the word (acute = high, macron = low), with the realisation of each tone depending on whether the marked syllable is a monosyllable, a non-final syllable, or the final syllable (the whole word carries a pitch contour determined by the tone and its position). Minimal pairs given on p. 15 (nomo 'you' vs nomo 'I', kase 'underarm' vs kase 'pith', sere 'mountain ridge / shoots / sun', ne 'you' vs ne 'mosquito'). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the grammar (full scanned of printed pp. 5-106 searched for stress, accent, prominence, pitch, intonation); the only related entry is the glossary definition 'tone: pitch; tune'. So the work makes no statement about word stress at all, neither its presence nor its absence.
new_statements.exceptions: none for tone; the grammar refers the compiler to May & Loeweke 1965 (Anthropological Linguistics 7(5)) for the full phonology, which is not open
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar (printed pp. 7-8) describes two dialects of Fasu (Namo Me): the Kaipu/Sisipia/Kewotiki dialect (with vowel harmony in verb suffixes) and the dialect southeast of the Aiyo River (Ririku, Aiyo, Mano, Anuwape, Tamatiki, etc.), with intermediate villages (Yorokopayu, Upoko, Sonaketiki, Yakifu, Hepaya); the phonology section does not say which dialect the tone description is based on, and states the data were collected 1961-1976. Total speakers about 1,000 at the time. 'Fasu' is the government name; speakers prefer Namo Me; older names Kaibu/Kaipu, Fasu-Kaibu, Namumi, Namomebo.

sources.note: '"word tone" in Fasu (May and Loeweke 1965..) is described as only one tonal contrast per word, and this tonal contrast is located on the "nuclear" (stressed) syllable, which may be any of the syllables in mono-, di-, or trisyllabic words, with tones on other syllables being predictable.' Gives minimal pairs e.g. kéno 'tail' vs kenó 'collarbone'.
